1. Model consistently overestimates prices, especially in the early part of the forecast horizon — adjust downward by 2–5% for the first 5–10 days.

2. After sharp price spikes (e.g., >70), model tends to overshoot and fail to correct — reduce forecast by 3–8% in the following 3–5 days.

3. Model exhibits mean reversion bias — if price is above 75, forecast should be capped at 75–78; if below 65, floor at 63–67.

4. Forecast lags true price movements by 1–3 days — shift forecast down by 1–2 units for the first 3 days if true price is trending down.

5. Model underestimates volatility in low-price zones — if history shows 60–65 range, forecast should be 5–10% higher than actual to account for downward momentum.

6. Avoid linear extrapolation — if true price drops after a spike, model should not continue rising — introduce a “cool-down” slope or step-down correction after peak.

7. For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overfit recent high prices — use 10-day moving average or weighted average of last 10 days to anchor forecast.
